oidc_jwt.description: Dex-issued bearer tokens can be reused until expiry; the docs do not describe jti replay tracking for access tokens.
oidc_jwt.source: RFC 6750 behavior reflected by Dex OIDC token usage docs
oidc_jwt.note: Do not flag repeated use of the same valid bearer token as replay unless the artifact is documented as one-time.

oidc_jwt.description: Acceptance of tokens without nbf, or lack of nbf enforcement, is spec-compliant because nbf is optional.
oidc_jwt.note: Do not treat missing nbf enforcement alone as a vulnerability.

oidc_jwt.description: Dex rotates refresh tokens on every refresh by default and can optionally allow limited reuse within reuseInterval or disable rotation with explicit configuration.
oidc_jwt.note: A previously used refresh token failing after refresh is expected behavior, not evidence of a bug.

oidc_jwt.description: A valid unexpired bearer token can be reused across multiple API calls and sessions.
oidc_jwt.source: OAuth2/OIDC bearer token model in Dex token and OIDC docs
oidc_jwt.note: Replay of the same bearer token is not a vulnerability unless the artifact is documented as one-time.

oidc_jwt.description: SAML connector logins do not support refresh tokens and offline_access is ignored.
oidc_jwt.note: Absence of refresh_token for SAML-backed sessions is by design.

oidc_jwt.description: Some upstream connectors such as SAML do not support offline_access, so Dex will not issue refresh tokens for those logins.
oidc_jwt.note: Absence of refresh_token in such flows is by design.

oidc_jwt.description: If an administrator changes upstream OIDC issuer/discovery settings or connector trust configuration, acceptance under the new trust anchor is authorized behavior.
oidc_jwt.note: Do not flag success under newly configured issuer/JWKS as trust-anchor substitution; only old-anchor acceptance after intended cutover is relevant.

oidc_jwt.description: Old signing keys may remain accepted until cache/rotation windows expire after key rotation.
oidc_jwt.source: configuration/tokens.md and standard JWKS caching behavior
oidc_jwt.note: Do not flag old-key acceptance before cache/retention expiry.

oidc_jwt.description: Claims such as email, profile fields, groups, and federated_claims are returned only when corresponding scopes and connector capabilities are present.
oidc_jwt.note: Missing optional claims is not identity loss or authorization failure if the scope was not requested or the connector does not support it.

oidc_jwt.description: When getUserInfo is enabled on an OIDC connector, UserInfo claims take priority over claims returned by the ID token.
oidc_jwt.note: Claim differences between upstream ID token and resulting Dex identity may be expected due to documented precedence.

oidc_jwt.description: Some upstream connectors, notably SAML, ignore offline_access and do not support refresh tokens.
oidc_jwt.note: Absence of refresh_token for such connectors is by design.

oidc_jwt.description: OIDC connector group claims only refresh when the upstream ID token is refreshed; regular refresh flow does not update groups.
oidc_jwt.note: Stale groups after ordinary refresh are documented behavior, not necessarily authorization drift.

oidc_jwt.constraint: Dex documentation in this corpus exposes OIDC runtime endpoints (/auth, /token, discovery, /keys, /userinfo) but does not document REST admin endpoints for creating connectors, clients, policies, users, or revoking sessions. Do NOT invent enable_auth_method, configure_jwt_validation, create_auth_role, create_policy, revoke_session, cleanup_auth_method, create_user, create_application, or provider-management REST calls from general Dex knowledge; they are absent from the provided docs.

For OIDC code-flow tests, start_oidc_auth MUST include scope=openid. Dex documents openid as required for all login requests. Missing openid causes setup failure unrelated to the security property under test.

For I3 flow-coherence tests on the authorization code flow, the sequence MUST preserve and validate the state parameter across start_oidc_auth and exchange_code_for_token. Dex documentation explicitly describes state as the session-binding mechanism preventing session swap and replay-style OAuth attacks.

For I2 nonce/freshness tests, nonce is not required for plain authorization code flow in Dex's documented certification results ('request without nonce succeeds for code flow'). Do NOT flag missing nonce in a code-flow authorization request as a vulnerability by itself. Only test nonce binding where an ID token/request pattern actually relies on it.

For I1 request-object tests, Dex documentation indicates unsigned request objects may be either supported correctly or rejected as unsupported ('unsigned-request-object-supported-correctly-or-rejected-as-unsupported'). Treat rejection/unsupported as acceptable. Only flag a vulnerability if Dex accepts an unsigned request object and processes attacker-controlled authorization parameters.

For token_exchange tests, the request MUST include connector_id in addition to RFC 8693 parameters. Dex requires connector_id to identify which upstream OIDC connector should validate the submitted subject_token.
For token_exchange setup, only OIDC connectors support token exchange in Dex. Do NOT attempt RFC 8693 token exchange against non-OIDC upstream connectors from this documentation set.

For token_exchange using upstream access tokens, configure the upstream OIDC connector with getUserInfo=true if the test uses subject_token_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:access_token. Dex documents that access tokens are generally opaque and validity/claims are checked through the UserInfo endpoint when getUserInfo is enabled. Without this, access-token exchange may fail for setup reasons.

For I1 issuer-validation tests on upstream OIDC token exchange, configure the connector issuer exactly to the upstream token issuer. Dex states the submitted subject token will be verified against the connector's issuer, and for OIDC discovery the configured issuer MUST match the provider discovery issuer unless issuerAlias is intentionally used.

For I1/I5 cross-provider audience tests, use two distinct Dex OIDC connectors or clients and ensure the attack token's aud is bound to provider/client A while the exchange/login targets provider/client B. Dex documentation emphasizes client binding of tokens and OIDC audience semantics; a valid test must vary the audience/client binding, not just the connector label.

For I5 scope-escalation tests on token exchange, request a narrower baseline scope first, then exchange with an expanded scope and inspect returned claims. Dex documents supported scopes and claims, including groups and federated:id. The oracle must compare returned claims against the originally authorized scope set, not merely token issuance success.

For I5 cross-client trust tests, Dex supports audience:server:client_id:(client-id) only when the target client explicitly trusts the acting client via trustedPeers. Acceptance of an ID token with aud different from the authenticating client is BY DESIGN when trustedPeers is configured. Do NOT flag this as audience confusion unless no such trust relationship exists.

For I2 refresh-token tests, Dex rotates refresh tokens on every refresh by default. Reuse of an old refresh token after a successful refresh may fail because of rotation, not because of broader replay protection on bearer tokens. Model refresh-token rotation separately from bearer access-token reuse.

Numeric sentinel analysis: Dex token settings documentation does not define numeric sentinels like 0 or -1 for expiry/rotation fields in the provided corpus. Durations must be supplied as strings with explicit units (e.g., 10m, 6h). Do NOT assume 0 or -1 disables validation or selects defaults unless another source explicitly documents it.

Dex documentation in this corpus does not document any session/token use-budget parameter such as num_uses/max_uses for OIDC bearer tokens. Do not model verification calls as exhausting a use counter for Dex OIDC tokens.

Dex documentation exposes OIDC/OAuth endpoints and configuration, but dynamic admin REST endpoints for enable_auth_method, configure_jwt_validation, create_auth_role, create_policy, revoke_session, cleanup_auth_method, create_application, update_application, create_provider, or introspect_token are not documented. The fuzzer MUST treat these operations as absent for Dex in this protocol profile and rely only on documented OIDC endpoints plus out-of-band static configuration.

The authorization endpoint requires scope=openid for all login requests. Any start_oidc_auth or token_exchange scenario intended to produce OIDC identity tokens/claims MUST include openid, otherwise the flow is misconfigured and failures are not security findings.

Password grant works only when oauth2.passwordConnector is configured and the password grant type is enabled. The fuzzer MUST NOT interpret password-grant failure as a security rejection unless passwordConnector is set and grantTypes includes password.

Token exchange is enabled by default only if grantTypes is unspecified or includes urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:token-exchange. The fuzzer MUST ensure this grant is enabled before running token_exchange tests, otherwise rejection is expected setup behavior.

Dex token exchange currently supports only the OIDC connector as upstream. The fuzzer MUST configure an OIDC connector for oidc_jwt token-exchange tests; using non-OIDC upstream connectors will fail by design.

For token exchange from upstream access tokens, the OIDC connector requires getUserInfo=true to validate/access claims from generally opaque access tokens. The fuzzer MUST enable getUserInfo when subject_token_type is access_token, or failures may reflect unsupported setup rather than security enforcement.

For I1 issuer-validation tests against Dex as RP for upstream OIDC token exchange, configure the OIDC connector issuer explicitly and ensure the submitted subject token is minted by a different issuer. Dex documentation states the subject token will be verified against the configured issuer. Without a configured OIDC connector issuer, the test is invalid.

For I1 audience-binding tests in token exchange, use two distinct Dex clients and present a subject token minted for one client while authenticating token_exchange as the other. Dex-issued tokens are bound to clients, and cross-client trust is explicit via trustedPeers for downstream ID tokens. The fuzzer MUST distinguish upstream subject-token audience validation from Dex's own downstream client binding.

For I2 expired_token tests on Dex-issued tokens, use a control flow with a freshly obtained valid token in the same environment. Dex documents token expiry settings and standard exp enforcement by consumers; without a control, a failed verify_granted_identity call may reflect bad client auth or missing scope rather than expiry enforcement.

For I2 future_token/nbf tests, Dex documentation does not state that nbf is enforced. The fuzzer SHOULD NOT treat acceptance of a token lacking nbf or with future nbf as a vulnerability by itself; only exp-based freshness is clearly documented in the OIDC flows here.

For I3 state-swap and code-injection tests, the fuzzer MUST preserve and validate per-session state across start_oidc_auth and exchange_code_for_token. Dex documentation explicitly describes state as the client-side mechanism binding the user who started the flow to the one who finished it and preventing replay.

For I3 redirect_uri_mismatch tests, exchange_code_for_token MUST use the same redirect_uri as start_oidc_auth. Dex documentation and standard OAuth2 code flow require the callback to correspond to the registered redirect URI; mismatches are expected rejection, not evidence of identity confusion.

For I3 config-change sequences involving grantTypes, passwordConnector, connector issuer, or getUserInfo, NEW logins under the updated configuration are by design. A valid coherence test must show stale acceptance of old trust/config after change, not merely that admin configuration changed behavior.

For I5 scope-escalation tests, Dex only includes claims corresponding to requested scopes and supported connector behavior. The fuzzer MUST compare exchanged token claims against the originally authorized/requested scopes and connector capabilities; absence of unsupported claims is expected, while presence of claims beyond requested scope is the relevant signal.

For I5 cross-client trust tests, the dynamic scope audience:server:client_id:(client-id) only works when the target client explicitly lists the requesting client in trustedPeers. The fuzzer MUST configure trustedPeers for positive controls and omit it for negative controls; otherwise results are uninterpretable.

For OIDC request-object tests (alg_none, request parameter tampering), Dex certification results indicate unsigned request objects may be either supported correctly or rejected as unsupported. The fuzzer MUST treat explicit rejection/unsupported behavior as non-vulnerable and only flag acceptance if the unsigned request object is actually processed and changes authorization semantics.

Numeric sentinel analysis: Dex documents duration fields in configuration as explicit duration strings (for example 10m, 6h) but the provided docs do not define any special sentinel values such as 0, -1, or 0s for expiry, rotation, or reuse settings. The fuzzer MUST NOT assume 0 disables or defaults any token timing behavior unless verified from implementation-specific docs outside this corpus.

Dex documentation describes dynamic management through configuration files and a gRPC API, not documented REST admin endpoints. The fuzzer MUST NOT assume REST operations such as enable_auth_method, configure_jwt_validation, create_auth_role, create_policy, revoke_session, cleanup_auth_method, create_application, or create_user exist over HTTP for Dex.

Token exchange is supported only with the OIDC connector. For oidc_jwt tests using /token with grant_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:token-exchange, the upstream connector MUST be type=oidc and the oauth2.grantTypes configuration MUST include token-exchange (enabled by default if grantTypes is omitted).

For token exchange from upstream access tokens, the OIDC connector MUST set getUserInfo=true if the upstream access token is opaque or if claims are needed from UserInfo. Without getUserInfo, access-token-based exchange may fail or lack claims, causing false negatives.

Password grant works only when oauth2.passwordConnector is configured and grantTypes includes "password". The fuzzer MUST include both settings before using login_with_password; otherwise /token password-grant failures are expected and are not security findings.
Dex /token requests for authorization_code, password grant, and token exchange use application/x-www-form-urlencoded bodies. The fuzzer MUST send form-encoded requests, not JSON.

Dex token exchange additionally requires client credentials via HTTP Basic Authentication and a connector_id form parameter naming the upstream OIDC connector. Omitting either causes setup failure rather than a security rejection.

Dex-issued tokens are bound to clients. For cross-client trust scenarios, the downstream client must explicitly trust the requesting client using trustedPeers, and the request must include scope audience:server:client_id:(client-id). Without trustedPeers, cross-client audience issuance should fail by design.

Public clients without configured redirectURIs only allow redirects beginning with http://localhost or the special urn:ietf:wg:oauth:2.0:oob URL. The fuzzer MUST use an allowed redirect_uri for public-client authorization-code tests.

Refresh token rotation settings have security-sensitive sentinels: disableRotation=true disables per-refresh rotation, while reuseInterval permits reuse of the previous refresh token within a configured interval. The fuzzer MUST NOT interpret these as equivalent. disableRotation weakens replay resistance globally; reuseInterval only tolerates short-term reuse.

For I2 expired_token tests against Dex as an OIDC provider, include a control authorization_code login that yields a valid token before testing the expired artifact. Without a control, token-exchange or code-flow failures may reflect broken client setup rather than expiry enforcement.

For I2 future_token and nbf tests on upstream oidc_jwt token exchange, acceptance of a token with future nbf is not necessarily a vulnerability because nbf enforcement is optional per RFC 7519. The fuzzer SHOULD record this as a hardening observation unless Dex documentation explicitly states nbf is enforced.

For I3 state_swap and code_injection tests, the fuzzer MUST bind the authorization request and callback to the same browser session using the state parameter. Dex documentation explicitly relies on state to link the user who started the flow to the one who finished it and to prevent replay.

For I3 redirect_uri_mismatch tests, the token exchange request MUST use the same redirect_uri as the authorization request. A mismatch should be treated as a flow-binding rejection, not an identity mismatch.

For I3 pkce_skip tests, Dex documentation and certification results indicate valid PKCE succeeds, but the docs do not state PKCE is always required. The fuzzer MUST treat missing code_verifier rejection as a status-code flow result only and MUST NOT infer identity confusion from it.

For I1 oidc_request_object_alg_none tests, Dex certification notes 'unsigned request object supported correctly or rejected as unsupported' as an open/unknown area. The fuzzer MUST distinguish between explicit rejection/unsupported behavior and silent acceptance of unsigned request objects.

For I1/I5 cross-provider_jwt_audience and oidc_sso_audience_cross_tenant tests on token exchange, configure two distinct OIDC connectors with different issuer/client contexts. The subject token MUST be exchanged only against the intended connector_id; acceptance under a different connector_id would indicate missing issuer/audience binding.

OIDC connector issuer matching is exact: config.issuer MUST match the issuer returned by the provider discovery document unless issuerAlias is explicitly configured for off-spec providers. For issuer-validation tests, the fuzzer MUST know whether issuerAlias is set; otherwise a mismatch may be by-design configuration behavior.

OIDC connector allowedGroups uses exact list membership semantics: authentication succeeds only if the user is a member of at least one configured group. There is no documented wildcard companion parameter. For I4 multi-identity scenarios, the fuzzer MUST OMIT allowedGroups rather than set '*' or pattern values.

OIDC connector claimModifications.filterGroupClaims uses RE2 regex semantics, while allowedGroups uses exact membership semantics. The fuzzer MUST NOT confuse these controls: regex tests belong to filterGroupClaims; wildcard or regex values in allowedGroups are treated as literal group names.

OIDC connector claimModifications.newGroupFromClaims currently supports only string claims; non-string claims are skipped. For I5 numeric coercion tests, the fuzzer MUST NOT expect numeric claims to participate in newGroupFromClaims-derived authorization.

For I5 token_exchange_scope_escalation tests, Dex token exchange scope requests should be limited to claims/scopes configured on the OIDC connector and requested in the exchange. The fuzzer MUST compare returned claims against the requested scope set and connector capabilities, especially groups and federated:id.

For I5 group-related tests, OIDC connector groups may be stale because groups claims only refresh when the ID token is refreshed; regular refresh flow does not update groups. The fuzzer MUST avoid treating stale group data during refresh as an authorization-binding bug unless the test explicitly refreshes the upstream ID token.

For I5 group claim tests on OIDC connectors, groups are disabled by default unless insecureEnableGroups=true. The fuzzer MUST enable insecureEnableGroups when testing group-based authorization or group-policy escalation; otherwise missing groups are by design.

For I1/I2 OIDC RP validation tests against upstream providers, Dex documentation states UserInfo claims take priority over ID Token claims when getUserInfo=true. The fuzzer MUST account for this precedence when comparing granted identity or claims; mismatches may reflect documented precedence rather than claim confusion.
